name: Forward head posture exercises

lead: Forward head posture (also called nerd neck or tech neck) is when the head sits ahead of the shoulders. Exercise routines aim to bring the head back over the shoulders, giving a cleaner side profile, a better neck line and a more upright look.

Programmes strengthen the deep neck flexors and shoulder-blade muscles and stretch tight neck and chest muscles. Forward head posture is quantified by the craniovertebral angle, and a trial found neck exercises improved the ability of people with chronic neck pain to hold an upright posture during a task. A meta-analysis found an association between the posture and neck pain in adults. In forums, some users say pulling the head back makes a recessed chin look weaker, while others expect a better profile; no study has examined the appearance claims.

paras: People do chin tucks, deep neck flexor work, rows and other upper-back strengthening, plus chest and neck stretches, as a regular routine, often alongside posture reminders at the desk.

Exercise itself is generally low risk. Sources do not establish that exercise permanently changes head position or appearance, and the link between the posture and pain is mixed, with an association found in adults but not adolescents.

angle.text: Chin tucks and neck-strengthening routines build the muscles that hold the head over the shoulders, giving a cleaner profile and neck line. The exercises are studied for neck pain, and the community debates how pulling the head back changes the look of a recessed chin.

lead: Forward head posture (FHP) is a posture in which the head sits forward of the shoulders, often accompanied by rounded shoulders and increased upper-back curvature. It is commonly called text neck, tech neck or nerd neck, and is measured clinically with the craniovertebral angle [1][2]. Exercises for it typically aim to strengthen the deep neck flexors and shoulder-blade retractors and to stretch tight neck and chest muscles [3].

Research has examined the association of FHP with neck pain and headache and tested exercise regimens in people with neck pain [2][4][5]. A systematic review and meta-analysis found a relationship between FHP and neck pain in adults [6].

In looksmaxxing forums, FHP is discussed as affecting side-profile and overall posture, and some users argue that correcting it can make a recessed chin look weaker. No published study has examined these appearance claims.
infobox: Forward head posture, upper crossed pattern

paras: Wikipedia describes FHP as a hunched, kyphotic upper spine with the head carried forward, common among people who spend long hours at devices and in certain occupations [3]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, describes measurement by the craniovertebral angle, with values below 50 degrees taken to indicate FHP, and repeats a widely cited estimate that load on the neck rises as the head moves forward [1]. The upper crossed pattern combines tight upper trapezius, levator scapulae and pectoral muscles with weak deep neck flexors [1].

Programmes commonly described include strengthening the deep neck flexors and mid and lower back muscles, stretching the upper trapezius and chest, breaks from sustained postures, and ergonomic changes [3]. Thoracic manipulation has also been studied for neck pain [3].
A trial of 58 people compared two neck-exercise regimens for the ability of people with chronic neck pain to maintain an upright cervical and thoracic posture during a distracting task [4].

A cross-sectional study of 62 people with neck pain and 52 without examined head posture measured by the craniovertebral angle in relation to pain and disability [2]. Older studies reported differences in head posture and upper cervical flexor performance in people with cervical headache and in tension-type headache and migraine [7][8][9].
A 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis examined the relationship between forward head posture and neck pain [6]. Wikipedia summarises it as finding a link in adults but not adolescents [3].

An observational study of office workers compared neck and shoulder postures between symptomatic and asymptomatic people [10], and an earlier study examined postural abnormalities and pain in healthy adults [11]. No studies found testing whether FHP exercises change facial appearance, jaw or chin profile.

One looksmax.org thread suggests FHP is common among models and actors and asks whether correcting it is unnecessary; a reply says they may pose that way for photos, and another user wonders about links to maxillary growth after gaming through adolescence. Another thread cites an article on health problems associated with FHP and reports that good head posture becomes natural over time. A third argues that people with a recessed chin or jaw hold the head forward to open the airway, and that tucking the chin back makes the chin look worse.
Proponents of correction cite pain and posture; those wary of it cite profile aesthetics. The sources reviewed do not test either position.

lore.intro: Forum discussion of forward head posture splits between those who treat it as a flaw to fix and those who question whether fixing it helps looks.
